one_line: A phase 1b clinical trial demonstrated that the tau-targeting antisense oligonucleotide MAPT Rx was well-tolerated and significantly reduced cerebrospinal fluid tau levels in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease.
summary: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 1b trial, researchers evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetics, and target engagement of MAPT Rx, a tau-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (ASO), in 46 patients with mild Alzheimer's disease. Participants received intrathecal bolus administrations of MAPT Rx (10 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg monthly, or 115 mg quarterly) or placebo over a 13-week treatment period. The study found that MAPT Rx was generally well-tolerated, with adverse events being mostly mild to moderate, the most common being post-lumbar puncture headaches. Treatment resulted in dose-dependent decreases in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) total tau and p-tau181 concentrations. Notably, mean reductions of greater than 50% from baseline were observed at 24 weeks post-last dose in the higher dose groups. The findings demonstrate proof-of-concept for antisense-mediated suppression of tau protein synthesis in the central nervous system.

key_claims.claim: MAPT Rx is well-tolerated and safe for administration in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease.
key_claims.evidence: Adverse events were reported in 94% of MAPT Rx-treated patients and 75% of placebo-treated patients; all were mild or moderate. No serious adverse events were reported in MAPT Rx-treated patients.

key_claims.claim: MAPT Rx leads to a dose-dependent and sustained reduction in CSF total tau and p-tau181 levels.
key_claims.evidence: Mean percentage change from baseline in t-tau concentration at 8 weeks post-last dose was −30%, −40%, −49% and −42% in MAPT Rx 10 mg, 30 mg and 60 mg monthly and 115 mg quarterly groups, respectively; CSF t-tau continued to decline at 24 weeks post-last dose showing −56% and −51% mean percentage change from baseline in the 60 mg and 115 mg groups.
key_claims.location: Exploratory endpoints / Concentration of t-tau in CSF / Figure 3

key_claims.claim: MAPT Rx treatment causes greater increases in ventricular volume compared to placebo.
key_claims.evidence: Mean change from baseline in ventricular volume (VV) as a percentage of total intracranial volume 6 months post-baseline was greater in the 10 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg and 115 mg MAPT Rx dose groups (0.5%, 0.7%, 0.7% and 0.6%, respectively) than that observed in the placebo group (0.2%).

methods.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multiple-ascending dose phase 1b trial
methods.population: Adults aged 50-74 with mild Alzheimer's disease (CDR 1 or 0.5 with Memory 1, MMSE 20-27)
methods.duration: 13-week treatment period followed by a 23-week post-treatment period

funding_and_conflicts: Funded by Ionis Pharmaceuticals and Biogen. Multiple authors are employees of and hold stock in Ionis or Biogen. Several other authors report advisory board memberships, consultancies, and research grants from various pharmaceutical companies including Biogen, Roche, and Ionis.
limitations: Small sample size (N=46) typical of Phase 1 trials.
Lack of diversity, as all study participants were white.
Relatively young patient population (mean age 66, almost half diagnosed before age 65), which may not perfectly represent typical late-onset AD.
Short duration (13-week treatment period) limits the ability to assess clinical efficacy or long-term safety.
red_flags: Quantitative assessment of ventricular volume showed greater increases in MAPT Rx treatment groups compared to placebo (up to 0.7% vs 0.2%), which was discussed as potential 'pseudoatrophy' but warrants closer longitudinal monitoring.
